content: Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) are a cornerstone in the treatment of asthma, functioning as anti-inflammatory agents within the airways of the lungs. These medications provide significant benefits, such as improved symptom control and enhanced lung function. However, they are also associated with potential adverse effects, both locally (e.g., in the mouth and throat) and systemically (e.g., effects on bone density or adrenal function). Ciclesonide is a newer corticosteroid that is converted into its active form directly within the lungs, which may help reduce local side effects compared to other ICS. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and side effect profile of ciclesonide in comparison to other inhaled corticosteroids for the management of chronic asthma. The review included randomized studies that compared ciclesonide to other ICS, either at equivalent doses or at lower doses of ciclesonide. A total of 21 trials involving 7,243 participants were analyzed. When ciclesonide was compared to beclomethasone dipropionate (BDP) or budesonide (BUD) at equivalent daily doses, the results for peak expiratory flow (PEF) were similar. However, forced vital capacity (FVC) was found to be higher with ciclesonide. Data on forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) were inconsistent across studies. Rates of treatment withdrawal and symptom control were comparable between ciclesonide and BDP/BUD. When compared to fluticasone propionate (FP) at the same dose, there were no significant differences in lung function parameters, including FEV1, FVC, and PEF. Notably, pediatric quality of life scores were better with ciclesonide. Additionally, the incidence of oral candidiasis (a fungal infection in the mouth) was lower with ciclesonide, although other side effects did not show significant differences between treatments. When lower doses of ciclesonide were compared to BDP or BUD, the difference in FEV1 was not statistically significant, but the possibility of a meaningful advantage for BDP/BUD could not be ruled out. Other lung function outcomes showed no significant differences between the treatments, and pediatric quality of life scores were similar. Adverse events occurred at comparable rates between ciclesonide and BDP/BUD. In three studies comparing ciclesonide to FP at half the nominal dose, FEV1 was not significantly different between the treatments. However, the results did not demonstrate equivalence, as the confidence intervals suggested some uncertainty (-0.05 L, 95% CI -0.11 to 0.01). The authors concluded that ciclesonide appears to be an equivalent treatment option to other ICS at similar nominal doses, particularly for patients requiring low-dose steroid therapy. However, at half the dose of FP or BDP/BUD, the effects of ciclesonide were less consistent. The reduced incidence of oral candidiasis with ciclesonide may be clinically relevant for patients who are prone to this side effect. Further research is needed to clarify the role of ciclesonide in asthma management, especially in pediatric populations. Additional studies comparing ciclesonide to FP at a dose ratio of 1:2 are a priority for future investigation.
